title: There is a kind of hunger that looks spiritual…
paragraphs:
There is a kind of hunger that looks spiritual…
but is deeply dangerous.

It doesn’t reject God.
It doesn’t mock His power.
It actually wants it.
But it wants it for the wrong reason.
That was Simon.
In Acts of the Apostles chapter 8, Simon the Sorcerer saw something that shook him.

He had already amazed people with his magic.
He had influence.
He had attention.
He had a reputation.
Scripture says people once called him “the great power of God.”
But then something changed.
He encountered the real power of God through the apostles—through Philip the Evangelist, and later through Peter the Apostle and John the Apostle.

And suddenly…
his old power looked small.

So he believed.
He was baptized.
He followed closely.
From the outside, it looked right.
But heaven sees deeper than appearances.
Because when Simon saw the apostles lay hands on people and the Holy Spirit was given…
he didn’t fall on his face in worship.
He reached for his wallet.

“Give me this power also,” he said,
“so that anyone I lay hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”
And then came one of the sharpest rebukes in Scripture:
“May your money perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God.”
Let that sink in.

Simon didn’t ask for money.
He didn’t ask for fame.
He asked for spiritual power.

And still…
he was completely wrong.
Why?
Because Simon revealed something many people still carry today:
He wanted power without surrender.

He wanted ability without transformation.
He wanted impartation without repentance.
And that is where things become dangerous.
Because not every desire for spiritual things is pure.

Some people want the anointing…
but not the crushing that produces it.

Some want to be used by God…
but do not want to be corrected by God.

Some want public power…
but avoid private surrender.
And Simon stands as a warning to all of us.

You can be around revival…
and still have a corrupted motive.

You can witness miracles…
and still crave attention.

You can believe…
and still be bound.
Peter discerned it immediately:

“Your heart is not right before God…
you are full of bitterness and captive to sin.”
That is heavy.
Because it means Simon’s issue was not ignorance.
It was misalignment of the heart.
And here is the part many people miss:
Simon didn’t deny God’s power.
He tried to use it.
That is the difference.

One posture bows.
The other leverages.

One says, “God, change me.”
The other says, “God, empower me… as I am.”
But God does not anoint unyielded ambition.

The Holy Spirit is not a tool.
He is not a force to be controlled.
He is not a shortcut to influence.
He is holy.
And holy things cannot be handled with unholy motives.
You cannot buy what only surrender can carry.
Read that again.
You cannot buy what only surrender can carry.

Simon offered silver…
because he still thought in transactions.
But the kingdom operates by transformation.

Not payment.
Not performance.
Not platform.
Transformation.
And here is the uncomfortable question this story forces us to face:
Why do you want what you’re asking God for?

Is it to glorify Him?
Or to elevate yourself?

Is it to serve?
Or to be seen?

Is it to become holy?
Or to become impressive?

Because those two paths may look similar at the start…
but they lead to very different outcomes.
Simon’s story is not just about a man in Samaria.
It is about a spirit that still exists today.

A spirit that wants visibility without purity.
Influence without obedience.
Spiritual language without spiritual death.
But the gospel does not offer power without a cross.
And the Spirit does not rest on pride.
If you truly want what God carries…
you must become what God can trust.

Broken.
Yielded.
Repentant.
Aligned.
Simon said, “Pray for me.”
But notice this:

He asked to escape consequences…
not to be transformed.
Even in fear, his response reveals something.
And that is another warning.

It is possible to feel conviction…
and still avoid true surrender.
But today, you can choose differently.

You can desire God—not for what He gives,
but for who He is.

You can seek His presence—not to be seen,
but to be changed.

You can pursue the Holy Spirit—not as power to display,
but as holiness to carry.
Because the truth is simple… and weighty:
The Holy Spirit is not for sale.

And God will not place His power
into hands that refuse His process.

Engagement Question:
Be honest—have you ever caught yourself wanting what God can do more than wanting God Himself?
